content_metadata.description: A detailed demonstration on the properties of concave mirrors including focal length, radius of curvature, and magnification by Dr. Boyd F. Edwards.

qAndA.answer: He is using a concave mirror.
qAndA.question: What kind of mirror is Dr. Boyd F. Edwards using in the demonstration?

qAndA.answer: The mirror has a focal length of 80 centimeters.
qAndA.question: What is the focal length of the mirror?
What are the two black objects that Dr. Boyd F. Edwards places on the floor?

qAndA.answer: The reflection enlarges, becoming very large when he reaches the focal point.
qAndA.question: What happens to Dr. Boyd F. Edwards' reflection as he moves towards the focal point?

qAndA.answer: The magnification of the reflection becomes less than one and the reflection remains inverted.
qAndA.question: What happens to the reflection after Dr. Boyd F. Edwards moves past the radius of curvature?

scenes.contextualRelevance: Dr. Boyd F. Edwards explains the concepts of focal length, radius of curvature, and magnification in concave mirrors.

narrativeProgression.description: Dr. Boyd F. Edwards explains that the focal length of a concave mirror is half of the radius of curvature.
Dr. Boyd F. Edwards starts moving towards a concave mirror while observing his reflection and explaining the properties of its reflection.
As Dr. Boyd F. Edwards approaches the focal point of the concave mirror, his reflection increases in size.
When Dr. Boyd F. Edwards reaches the focal point, his reflection becomes very large.
As Dr. Boyd F. Edwards moves past the focal point, his reflection flips and becomes inverted.
When Dr. Boyd F. Edwards reaches the radius of curvature, the magnification of his reflection becomes one.
As Dr. Boyd F. Edwards moves past the radius of curvature, the magnification of his reflection becomes less than one.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: This is a demonstration of the images formed by a convex mirror.
This is a concave mirror that is.
This mirror is concave in the sense, you can think of it as a cave,
it has like an opening to it, and that's the concavity.
This particular mirror has a focal length of 80 centimeters.
So between my two fingers here,
so parallel rays from infinity would come in and focus at this point
about 80 centimeters away from the mirror.
And as we discussed, the focal point is half of the radius of curvature.
So the radius of curvature must therefore be 160 centimeters about out to here.
And I've placed these two erasers here and here
at the approximate focal length and radius of curvature,
which is twice the focal length, for reference.
So what I'm going to do is start with my nose against the mirror
and then back up slowly explaining what the image looks like.
And then the cutaways will allow you to see from my perspective what we're seeing.
So my nose in the mirror, then backing up slowly, approaching the focal point,
and my image is enlarging. It's getting bigger.
At the focal point, the image gets huge,
and then just beyond the focal point,
you can see the image is still huge, but it's inverted.
And then as I move past the focal point toward the radius of curvature,
the image is shrinking in size until at the radius of curvature,
the image is now un-magnified. The magnification is one.
Beyond the radius of curvature, the magnification becomes less than one,
and the image is therefore reduced and still inverted.
